newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Lower rates not enough to tackle high NZD - Cullen.
newsitem.headline: Lower rates not enough to tackle high NZD - Cullen.

text.p: New Zealand Labour Party finance spokesman Michael Cullen said on Monday that calls for lower interest rates "missed the point" and other measures were required to tackle an overvalued New Zealand dollar.
Tightening the government's purse strings was the wrong way to deal with the overvalued New Zealand dollar, he said.
Cullen reiterated that the New Zealand dollar had become a one-way bet through being "systematically overvalued", and more than just a fall in interest rates was required to correct it.
"The longer a highly overvalued exchange rate is bedded in, the more difficult it will be to root it out because of the inflationary consequences," he said.

"Calls for dropping interest rates miss the point. The amount of fall required to affect the exchange rate would be quite possibly seriously counterproductive. It is the exchange rate itself which is the primary problem."

The Labour Party, which is negotiating with nationalist New Zealand First to form a government after an inconclusive general election in October, has said it will insist on Cullen as finance minister. NZ First is also negotiating with the
The recipe, if followed, would lead to continued social failure combined with growing economic imbalances, followed by an "inevitable and savage correction" a year to 18 months down the track.

"If we do not achieve a significant correction in the exchange rate before Christmas, then it is all too possible that the economic outlook could turn bleak indeed at some stage in 1997," Cullen warned.

Speaking to the Hutt Valley Chamber of Commerce, Cullen said industry groups holding a summit this week on the high value of the dollar had already concluded that the only solution was to constrain very tightly government spending.
"This is so much garbage," Cullen said. "It will not work, it cannot work, and it is based on the wrong analysis of the problem."

He said the prevalent analysis was that a somewhat looser fiscal stance, as Labour proposes, would oblige the Reserve Bank to jack up interest rates and hence the exchange rate to remove inflationary pressures.
"All this analysis points to is the failure of the present regime of economic management to deliver sustainable economic growth at anything like sensible macroeconomic settings."
He said there were various "highly orthodox and commonly practised ways" of addressing the overvalued exchange rate, but declined to go into detail.
Economic strategy should address infrastructural and industrial development, skills training, a national savings strategy and balanced fiscal policy, Cullen said.
